strengths: The mean-point correspondence is a simple, original, and useful construction for generating three-camera pose hypotheses from four correspondences. Reusing established five-point and P3P solvers offers a practical alternative to substantially more complex algebraic or learned homotopy methods.

The empirical evaluation is substantial: 90,000 camera triplets across 18 scenes and three datasets, with both PoseLib and GC-RANSAC. Ablations examine refinement, filtering, early non-minimal refitting, and correspondence perturbations. Supplementary experiments address noise, scene geometry, outliers, threshold sensitivity, and a stricter error metric covering all three camera pairs.

The results demonstrate useful operating points even against an enhanced baseline. In Table 3, 4p3v(M)+R+F+ENM approximately matches the enhanced five-point baseline on PhotoTourism (76.16 versus 76.20 AUC@10) while reducing runtime from 56.52 to 44.51 ms. The perturbed mean-point variant achieves the highest reported aggregate accuracy on all three datasets.

The paper explains its approximate nature and documents important failures of the unmodified affine solver. Code and archived data links, a separate validation scene, and implementation settings support reproducibility. Overall, the practical contribution and extensive supporting evidence favor weak acceptance.
weaknesses: The claim of consistently providing the best speed-accuracy trade-off is stronger than the comparisons establish. Figure 4 omits the five-point baseline with +R+F, although Table 2 shows these modifications substantially improve it. Against the fully enhanced baseline, the strongest proposed variant gains 0.94 AUC@10 points on PhotoTourism while taking 112.60 versus 56.52 ms; on Aachen, the gain is 0.31 points at 139.19 versus 76.86 ms. Runtime curves for the enhanced baseline and uncertainty estimates are needed to establish the smaller advantages.

The timing comparison with homotopy continuation has a material confound. Section 8.3 states that loading its weights/data takes approximately 45 ms and occurs once per RANSAC run, substantial relative to the reported 60–67 ms total runtimes. This overhead could be amortized across repeated estimations. The reported accuracy advantage remains meaningful, but the timing evidence does not isolate solver efficiency from initialization overhead.

The theoretical guarantee is limited to image-space correspondence error. Lemma 1 bounds the centroid-to-epipolar-line distance by the triangle radius, which can be large; it does not establish pose accuracy or convergence of refinement. Figure 9 also shows residual error with noiseless inputs. Thus, the evidence supports an effective approximate initializer, while the assertion that ENM makes scene dependence negligible remains an empirical observation on the tested configurations.

There are correctable reporting and reproducibility issues. Table 7 repeats all Cambridge statistics and runtimes between the affine and mean-point methods for both +R+F and +R+F+ENM, requiring verification. The manuscript also leaves the affine-matrix-to-calibrated-pose conversion and precise LM objective and parameterization insufficiently explicit, although the code links mitigate this concern.
